title: How Much Does an Ambulance Ride Cost? Ground and Air Ambulance Prices (2026)
summary: How much does an ambulance ride cost? See ground and air ambulance prices, what insurance and Medicare cover, and how to review or negotiate an ambulance bill.
body_markdown:
An ambulance ride can cost anywhere from a few hundred dollars to tens of thousands, and most people don't see the price until the bill arrives after a medical emergency. What you pay depends on whether it's a ground or air ambulance, the level of care you received, how far you traveled, where you live, and your health insurance. Whether you've just received an ambulance bill or want to know what your coverage would pay before an emergency, this guide explains how ambulance bills work, what ground and air ambulance rides typically cost, and what to do if your bill looks too high.


## How much does an ambulance ride cost?


There's no single national price for an ambulance ride, because each ambulance provider (often a city fire department, county emergency medical services agency, hospital, or private company) sets its own rates, and the total cost depends on several factors. A few published figures show the range:


- **Ground ambulance, what insurers pay:** a[FAIR Health analysis of private insurance claims](https://www.healthcaredive.com/news/ground-ambulance-costs-continue-to-soar-study-finds/619195/) found the average amount for an emergency advanced life support (ALS) base fee rose from $486 in 2017 to $758 in 2020, and the basic life support (BLS) base fee rose from $373 to $522. Those figures don't include mileage.
- **Ground ambulance, posted rates:** billed charges are often much higher than what insurers pay. In Escondido, California, the[fire department's ambulance fee schedule](https://escondido.gov/1257/Ambulance-Transport-Fees) effective July 1, 2026, lists a $4,399 base rate plus $41 per mile, $103 for oxygen, and $206 for treatment without transport.
- **Air ambulance:** the U.S. Government Accountability Office found the[median price charged in 2017](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-19-292) was about $36,400 for a helicopter transport and $40,600 for a fixed-wing flight, up more than 60% from 2012.


Your out-of-pocket costs depend on your insurance coverage. Medicare, Medicaid, and private health plans usually pay part of the bill when the ride is medically necessary, but deductibles, coinsurance, and out-of-network charges can still leave you with a large balance.


## What makes up an ambulance bill? Ambulance fees explained


Most ambulance bills combine a base rate, a mileage charge, and charges for supplies or treatment. The mileage charge usually counts loaded miles, meaning the distance traveled with you on board.


The base rate depends on the level of care:


- **Basic life support (BLS):** transport with emergency medical technicians who provide basic monitoring, oxygen, bandaging, and immobilization.
- **Advanced life support (ALS):** transport with paramedics and medical equipment for more advanced care, such as cardiac monitoring, IV lines, and medications. ALS costs more than BLS.


Common add-on charges include:


- Oxygen
- Advanced airway management
- Cardiac monitoring or an EKG
- Medications given during the ride
- Extra crew time on scene


Some providers also bill for treatment without transport, when paramedics treat you on scene but don't take you to the hospital. Many city and county emergency medical services post their ambulance fees online, so it's worth searching for your local provider's rates and pricing structure.


## Ground ambulance costs with and without insurance


Ground ambulances are a common source of surprise bills because the ambulance company is often out of network, even when the hospital is in network. A[Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker analysis](https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/brief/ground-ambulance-rides-and-potential-for-surprise-billing/) of 2018 claims from large employer plans found that 51% of emergency ground ambulance rides and 39% of non-emergency rides included an[out-of-network](https://www.withflex.com/blog/in-network-vs-out-of-network) charge.


### With private insurance


Your insurance policy's[deductible](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-a-deductible) and[coinsurance](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-coinsurance) usually apply to ambulance rides. If the ambulance provider is out of network with your insurance company, it may also bill you for the difference between its charge and what your plan pays, known as balance billing. Federal surprise-billing protections don't cover ground ambulances, so that balance can be substantial.


### With Medicare


Medicare Part B covers ground ambulance transportation when traveling another way could endanger your health and you need care at a hospital, critical access hospital, rural emergency hospital, or skilled nursing facility.[According to Medicare](https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/ambulance-services) , after the Part B deductible you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount.


### With Medicaid


Medicaid generally covers medically necessary ambulance transportation, but rules, prior-approval requirements, and copays vary by state. Check with your state Medicaid program if you're unsure what you'll owe.


### Without insurance


Uninsured patients are billed the provider's full rate. Some municipal ambulance services and nonprofit hospitals offer discounts, payment plans, or financial assistance, so ask the billing office what's available before you pay.


## Air ambulance costs: helicopters and fixed-wing flights


Air ambulances include helicopters, which are often used to fly patients from an accident scene or between nearby hospitals, and fixed-wing airplanes, which are used for longer transfers. They're far more expensive than ground transport because of aircraft, fuel, maintenance, specialized equipment, medical personnel, and round-the-clock readiness, operational expenses that providers build into their prices. A helicopter often flies a patient with a serious injury, for example from a car accident, to a trauma center.


The GAO's 2019 report found median charges of about $36,400 for a helicopter and $40,600 for a fixed-wing flight in 2017, and that more than two-thirds of air ambulance transports for privately insured patients were out of network. Cost drivers include:


- Distance flown
- Aircraft type
- Level of medical care on board
- Whether the flight is an emergency or a scheduled transfer


For a non-emergency transfer, many plans require prior authorization. Ask the provider for a written estimate of the air ambulance flight and ask your insurer whether the provider is in network before you agree to the flight, if you have the chance.


## The No Surprises Act and ambulance bills


The[No Surprises Act](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/nsa-keyprotections.pdf) protects people with most private health plans from surprise medical billing for emergency care and for out-of-network air ambulance services. For a covered air ambulance ride, you generally pay only your in-network cost sharing, such as your deductible and coinsurance, and the provider and your plan settle the rest.


Ground ambulances are not covered by the federal law. Some states have their own ground ambulance billing protections, but they vary and often don't apply to self-funded employer plans. If you get a large ground ambulance bill, ask your health plan whether any state protections apply.


## How to review and negotiate an ambulance bill


You usually can't compare prices in an emergency, but you can review the bill afterward. For scheduled, non-emergency transport, such as a transfer between facilities, ask for a written estimate in advance.


When you get the bill:


- Request an itemized statement showing the base rate, mileage, and every supply or service.
- Check the mileage against a map of your route.
- Make sure the level of care billed (BLS or ALS) matches your medical records.
- Compare the bill with your plan's Explanation of Benefits.


Common errors include duplicate charges, wrong patient or insurance details that cause a denial, and a ride coded as non-emergency when it was an emergency. If your insurer denied the claim, you can file an appeal with documentation that the ride was medically necessary.


If someone else caused the accident that led to your ambulance ride, the ambulance expense may be part of a personal injury claim against the responsible party's insurance, so keep your bills and medical records.


To lower what you owe, contact the billing office, explain any financial hardship, and ask whether they can reduce the charge, accept your plan's rate, or set up a payment plan without interest. Nonprofit hospitals and some public agencies have financial assistance policies for qualifying households.


## Planning for unexpected medical costs


You can't always predict an ambulance ride, but your coverage choices affect what you'll pay. During open enrollment, compare each plan's deductible, coinsurance, and[out-of-pocket maximum](https://www.withflex.com/blog/deductible-vs-out-of-pocket-maximum) , since the out-of-pocket maximum caps your out-of-pocket expenses for covered in-network care in a year. Our[PPO vs HDHP guide](https://www.withflex.com/blog/ppo-vs-hdhp) explains how those trade-offs work.


The exact price of an ambulance ride is hard to predict, but knowing how ambulance bills are built, how your insurance responds, and where federal protections apply can make an unexpected bill easier to handle.
